newsitem.title: CANADA: Ag Canada cuts Prairie wheat output, canola up.
newsitem.headline: Ag Canada cuts Prairie wheat output, canola up.

text.p: Agriculture Canada on Friday cut its Prairie wheat production forecast for crop year 1997/98 (Aug/July), while raising canola's output outlook.

"Wheat production was revised downward to account for an estimated 200,000 hectares (494,200 acres) which remained unharvested from the fall of 1996," Ag Canada's July supply and disposition report stated.
The report follows Statistics Canada's June 27 acreage estimate, which did not account for unharvested Prairie acres and has been the source of speculation among grain analysts.
Production of all types of wheat should total 28.97 million tonnes in 1996/97 (Aug/July), down five percent from Ag Canada's May estimate of 30.495 million tonnes.

The International Grains Council on Thursday forecast Canadian wheat output in the current crop year at 25.5 million tonnes from 27 million, due to "a major shift to canola, flaxseed and other more profitable crops."
Ag Canada's report noted the same trend but differed in its output expectations.
Overall, grain and oilseed production in 1996/97 was set at 65.7 million above the 10-year trend of 57 million tonnes.
Output in 1997/98 was pegged at 62.5 million tonnes, Ag Canada said.

While Canadian wheat output for 1997/98 was forecast to drop 13 percent to 26.17 million tonnes versus 28.97 in 1996/97, supplies were expected to decline two percent due to high carry-in stocks, Ag Canada said.
The CWB deferred 1.5 million tonnes of wheat sales due to difficulties loading ocean vessels at Pacific ports from January to March.
The CWB said the delays cost it at least C$15 million in demurrage fines.
"Due to less competition from Australia and Argentina, Canadian exports are expected to increase and 1997/98 ending stocks are expected todecrease significantly," Ag Canada said.
Milling wheat prices were expected to fall to C$171 to C$201 a tonne, in-store Vancouver or St. Lawrence River in the coming year compared to C$206 in the current year.
Despite a rise in durum wheat output in the coming crop year to a record 4.9 million tonnes, prices were also expected to rise on North African demand while Iranian needs drop.
Durum prices were pegged at C$223 to C$253 a tonne, in store Vancouver or St. Lawrence River versus C$236 this year.
Canola prices were expected to drop from this year's level to a range of C$380 to C$420 a tonne in store Vancouver compared to C$438 to C$443 in 1996/97.

Although canola output was expected to rise 26.7 percent to 6.335 million tonnes in 1997/98 from 5.0 million tonnes this year it was only expected to offset dwindling stocks by 14 percent as domestic crushing capacity continues to expand.
"Stronger export demand is expected to prevent a significant increase in carry-over stocks," Ag Canada added.
